name: Stift Stams
kurzbeschreibung: Cistercian abbey Stift Stams in the Oberinntal: founded in 1273, featuring a baroque abbey basilica, burial vault of the Tyrolean sovereigns, Bernardisaal, and monastery museum.
beschreibung:
Overview

The storied Cistercian abbey Stift Stams is located in the sunny Tiroler Oberland in the municipality of Stams, around 35 kilometres west of Innsbruck. Framed by the slopes of the Stubaier and Mieminger Alps, the imposing monastery complex forms one of the most significant religious, cultural, and architectural centres of western Austria. The landmark, visible from afar with its distinctive onion-domed towers, combines high medieval foundation history with magnificent baroque architecture. Today, the monastery is not only a vibrant place of monastic prayer and pastoral care, but also the home of the internationally renowned Skigymnasium Stams and a popular museum for sacred art treasures.

History & Architecture

The monastery was founded in 1273 by the Tyrolean sovereign Graf Meinhard II. von Görz-Tirol and his wife Elisabeth von Bayern. Elisabeth was the widow of the Hohenstaufen king Conrad IV and the mother of the ill-fated last Hohenstaufen, Conradin, who was executed in Naples in 1268. In memory of Conradin and as an eternal burial place for the House of Tyrol, the ruling couple founded the abbey for the Cistercian monks from Kaisheim. After severe destruction during the Peasants' Wars of 1525, looting by Saxon troops in 1552, and a devastating major fire in 1593, the monastery experienced its baroque golden age from the 17th century onwards. The Gothic abbey church was thoroughly transformed into baroque style from 1729 by Tyrolean court architect Georg Anton Gumpp. An artistic milestone is the monumental, early baroque Lebensbaum-Hochaltar (Tree of Life high altar, 1609–1613) by Bartholomäus Steinle featuring 84 carved saint figures. Set into the nave floor, the monastery houses the Österreichische Fürstengruft (Austrian Princes' Crypt): built between 1681 and 1684 under Abbot Edmund Zoz and adorned by sculptor Andreas Thamasch with gilded statues, Tyrolean sovereigns rest here, including Meinhard II., Herzog Friedrich IV. mit der leeren Tasche, Sigmund der Münzreiche, and Emperor Maximilian's consort Bianca Maria Sforza. Other highlights include the magnificent Bernardisaal with its elaborate ceiling frescoes and the Heilig-Blut-Kapelle with its famous forged rose gate dating from 1716. Pope John Paul II elevated the collegiate church to a papal Basilica minor in 1983.

Visit & Getting There

The abbey basilica, the Bernardisaal, and the monastery museum are accessible on guided tours or individually. During the summer season (June to September), hourly guided tours take place Monday to Saturday from 09:00 to 11:00 and 13:00 to 16:00 (on Sundays and public holidays from 13:00 to 16:00). The monastery museum is open Tuesday to Saturday from 10:00 to 12:00 and 14:00 to 17:00. In the winter half-year (October to May), a regular public guided tour is offered every Thursday at 16:00. Admission prices (2025/2026 season): abbey tour including museum for adults €13.50, seniors and groups €11.00, school pupils and students €7.00; museum-only visit in summer €8.00. Discount available with the Innsbruck Card. Arrival by public transport: take the ÖBB S-Bahn (S1 or REX) to Bahnhof Stams, from where a level walk of barely ten minutes (approx. 500 metres) leads to the abbey portal; alternatively, take VVT regional bus line 4166 directly to the stop Stams Stift. By car: via the Inntalautobahn A12, exit Mötz/Stams, then continue on the B171 for about two kilometres to the visitor car park right at the monastery grounds (Stiftshof 1).

Tips

The abbey basilica, the monastery shop, and the abbey gardens are barrier-free and easily accessible for wheelchairs and prams; for the staterooms in the upper convent wing, advance telephone registration is recommended for guests with mobility impairments so that assistance can be arranged. Be sure to visit the traditional Klosterladen: here the monks sell homemade specialities such as the Stamser monastery liqueur, fine fruit brandies from the abbey's own distillery, herbal teas, and monastery honey. In the baroque Orangery in the castle park, a café-restaurant invites visitors to linger after their tour.
